section_summary: This section opens with detailed Spanish inventories of Japanese diplomatic and consular property in Lima, followed by the protocol and extensive French-language inventory for the transfer of Japanese archives and effects in Tehran. The remaining documents report or debate Allied custody, examination, storage, sale, and financing arrangements for Japanese official property in China, Ireland, Denmark, Belgium, Morocco, Argentina, and Mexico. Several files reveal disagreements over policy—especially whether archives should be sent to Washington, whether movable property should be stored or sold, and how firmly to compel former Japanese officials to surrender records and assets.

subfiles.title: Continuation of List I: Inventory of Japanese Legation, Consulate, Residence, and Chancery Property in Lima
subfiles.from: Japanese Legation and Consulate in Lima
subfiles.about: Continues a numbered Spanish-language inventory of furniture, appliances, office equipment, films, books, and other property belonging to Japanese diplomatic and consular establishments in Lima.
subfiles.summary: The continuation completes the inventory of one residence and then separately lists the consul’s residence and chancery. It records household furniture, rugs, appliances, typewriters, cinematographic machines, Japanese films, office fittings, and sixty-six boxes or crates of miscellaneous articles. The inventory is dated at Lima on November 8, 1945.

subfiles.title: List II: Property Available to the Swedish Legation for Routine Protection Work
subfiles.about: Lists Japanese furniture and equipment placed at the Swedish Legation’s disposal for routine work connected with the protection of Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: The list identifies household, gardening, and office articles retained for Swedish protection work in Lima. Items include desks, chairs, rugs, cleaning equipment, typewriters, calculating machines, steel cabinets, and waste baskets. The list is dated November 8, 1945.

subfiles.title: Inventory of Boxes and Crates Belonging to the Japanese Legation and Consulate
subfiles.from: Japanese Legation and Consulate in Lima
subfiles.about: Describes the contents and ownership of numbered boxes and crates belonging to the Japanese Legation, Consulate, and individual Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: The inventory covers stationery, seals, decorative objects, kitchenware, silver, records of the 1940 looting of Japanese property in Peru, civil-registration files, and consular documents. It also identifies numerous crates as the personal property of M. Yodokawa, Hanami, M. Yonekura, Nomura, K. Okochi, and K. Kawauchi. The final listed box contains insignia of the Japanese Red Cross.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Beirut Regarding Japanese Archives
subfiles.about: Raises policy questions that must be decided before instructions can be drafted concerning Japanese archives in Lebanon.
subfiles.summary: Wadsworth was willing to draft the Beirut instruction but asked whether France should join the Allied committee controlling Japanese archives in Lebanon. He recommended against French participation unless France were admitted to similar committees elsewhere, noting that the principal Allied victors over Japan were the United States, Soviet Union, Great Britain, and China. He also asked whether those powers should participate with France in taking over German archives.

subfiles.title: Chungking Telegram on Taking Over Japanese Archives in China
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese Foreign Office arrangements for assuming custody of Japanese diplomatic and consular archives and property.
subfiles.summary: Special representatives were being sent to Shanghai, Nanking, and Tientsin, while resident delegates or local officials would act elsewhere. Other Allied powers would receive access after inventories were completed, with work expected to finish by the end of January in Shanghai and Nanking but later in places where Japanese troops remained armed. The embassy had found no British or Soviet request for access and could not locate the referenced instructions concerning German archives.

subfiles.title: Dublin Telegram on the Japanese Consul General’s Continued Refusal
subfiles.about: Reports that the Japanese consul general continued to reject Allied instructions for surrendering consular archives and property.
subfiles.summary: The former consul general presented orders from Tokyo requiring him to deliver archives and property but again refused the local Allied instruction because he claimed it exceeded those orders. He objected to being called the former consul general and demanded to see the American instructions. The legation recommended a firm order to obey, suspension of his funds, and delivery of bankbooks and data needed to verify the completeness of the surrender.

subfiles.title: Borton Memorandum Proposing an Addition to the Property Policy
subfiles.from: Hugh Borton, Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.about: Proposes language allowing the sale of Japanese government property when storage is impracticable while protecting officials’ private property from sale.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum suggests adding a sentence to the Special Projects Division’s proposed policy. Japanese government property could be sold when storage was impracticable, with proceeds placed in a trust account, but private property of Japanese officials should not then be sold. The proposed insertion was intended to answer the practical question of inadequate storage space.

subfiles.title: Special Projects Division Memorandum on Storage or Sale of Japanese Property
subfiles.to: LE, JK, JA, and FE divisions
subfiles.about: Requests interdivisional views on a general policy for storing or disposing of Japanese diplomatic and consular property.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum recommends storing official Japanese property unless quantities, space requirements, depreciation, or deterioration make storage impracticable. It contrasts the situation with German property because a Japanese government still existed and the October 25 directive called for transfer of physical custody rather than liquidation. Handwritten comments propose permitting sale of Japanese government property when necessary while withholding private officials’ property from sale.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Memorandum on Storage or Sale of Japanese Property
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the proposal for a uniform policy governing Japanese diplomatic and consular property.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate recommends storage as the normal rule, with exceptions for excessive quantities, impracticable space demands, depreciation, or deterioration. It notes that sale proceeds might sometimes have to be deposited in an appropriate account but argues against general liquidation. The Special Projects Division requests the views of the interested regional divisions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 174: Transfer of Japanese Archives and Property in Tehran
subfiles.from: Robert Rossow, Jr., for the United States ambassador in Tehran
subfiles.about: Reports the joint Allied transfer of Japanese diplomatic property and archives from Swedish custody to sealed storage in the former German Legation.
subfiles.summary: Representatives of China, Great Britain, the Soviet Union, the United States, and Sweden agreed that the Japanese material should be moved from a rented private basement to the German Legation’s basement. The transfer was completed under joint supervision, sealed on November 30, and documented by a protocol and inventory. The embassy also reports Harry S. Aldrich’s request for intelligence examination and recommends eventual shipment to a central location rather than a locally conducted inspection that might provoke Soviet complications.

subfiles.title: Tehran Protocol Acknowledging Delivery of Japanese Property and Archives
subfiles.from: Representatives of the United States, China, Great Britain, and the Soviet Union in Tehran
subfiles.about: Formally acknowledges Allied receipt from Sweden of Japanese diplomatic and consular property and archives listed in an annex.
subfiles.summary: The protocol records the transfer by the Royal Swedish Legation to representatives of the four Allied powers. It is dated at Tehran on November 30, 1945. Signatories include M. Williams Blake, A. T. H. Achourov, and Chen Hou-Yu, together with the British representative.

subfiles.title: Annexed Inventory of Japanese Diplomatic and Consular Property in Tehran
subfiles.to: Representatives of the United States, Great Britain, China, and the Soviet Union
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed French-language inventory of Japanese archives, furniture, equipment, household goods, weapons, vehicles, art, tableware, and boxed effects transferred in Tehran.
subfiles.summary: The inventory begins with locked safes, filing cabinets, boxes of chancery records, books, office furniture, printing machines, firearms, rugs, and household furnishings. It continues through a motorcycle, radios, cameras, typewriters, Japanese artworks, silver, porcelain services, glassware, cutlery, kitchen equipment, preserved foods, clothing, and game tables. Conditions are carefully noted, including moth, damp, breakage, missing parts, and repairs performed after prolonged storage in a humid room.

subfiles.title: British Embassy Letter Transmitting Foreign Office Views
subfiles.from: G. R. Ranken, British Embassy, Washington
subfiles.to: A. W. Clattenburg, Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits British Foreign Office guidance on Japanese official archives and property in the Western Hemisphere.
subfiles.summary: Ranken forwards an extract from instructions sent to British missions in the Western Hemisphere. He clarifies that the guidance concerns Japanese archives and property in the countries to which those missions were accredited and does not cover archives found in United States territory. He offers to discuss any issues arising from the statement.

subfiles.title: Extract from Foreign Office Telegram to British Missions in Latin America
subfiles.to: British diplomatic missions in Latin American countries
subfiles.about: Sets out British proposals for transporting Japanese archives, disposing of property, and funding the continued protection of Japanese nationals.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office favors transporting archives to Washington while reserving unrestricted British access. It recommends ending leases, selling or leasing Japanese-owned buildings, and selling movable official property other than archives, stamps, and seals. Sale proceeds would enter a jointly administered account, from which the protecting power could retain necessary funds for Japanese nationals.

subfiles.title: Department of State Reply to Ranken on Divergent American Policy
subfiles.about: Explains revised American policy favoring traveling examination teams, storage of movable property, and jointly controlled trustee accounts.
subfiles.summary: The Department reports that it no longer plans routinely to move Latin American Japanese archives to Washington and instead expects expert teams to examine selected collections locally. It favors storing movable official property unless cost, deterioration, or space makes that impracticable and objects to selling the private property of former Japanese officials. Japanese funds and sale proceeds should be placed in a joint trustee account that can reimburse protecting powers for routine work, subsistence, moving, storage, and lease expenses.

subfiles.title: Buenos Aires Airgram Requesting Authority to Dispose of Property
subfiles.about: Requests authority to dispose of Japanese property not needed in Argentina because storage space is a serious problem.
subfiles.summary: The embassy refers to earlier correspondence concerning the former Japanese Legation’s property and archives. It reports that the British have received authority to dispose of unnecessary property. Cabot asks for comparable American authorization because continued storage requires considerable space.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 974: Custody of Japanese Property and Archives in Belgium
subfiles.about: Reports progress toward joint Four-Power custody and inventory of Japanese diplomatic and consular property in Belgium.
subfiles.summary: The four Allied embassies notified Belgium of their instructions, and Belgian officials raised no objection to replacing the Swedish Legation as custodian. Representatives began inventorying the Japanese Embassy at Brussels, which also contained material transferred from the Antwerp consulate, and planned to seal the documentary material pending expert examination. Patterson asks how caretaker, repair, and heating expenses should be paid and reports Soviet interest in purchasing or renting the embassy building and dividing its contents.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2067: Further Refusal of the Japanese Consul General in Dublin
subfiles.about: Forwards correspondence documenting the Japanese consul general’s continued resistance to Allied surrender instructions.
subfiles.summary: Gray states that the consul general remained unwilling to accept the authority of local American and British representatives despite Japan’s unconditional surrender and explicit orders from Tokyo. The consul wished to return home but continued to claim equal standing with the Allied officers and resisted their information demands. Gray and the British representative request that Allied headquarters direct the Japanese Foreign Office to order full cooperation.

subfiles.title: Japanese Consulate-General Cover Note Forwarding the December 3 Memorandum
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum concerning surrender of consular archives and property and the return of Japanese consular officers to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The brief note sends the American minister a copy of the consulate’s memorandum of the same date. It particularly draws attention to the translated instruction requiring notification of the American and British representatives. The note is initialed on behalf of the consul general.

subfiles.title: Japanese Memorandum on Surrender and Repatriation
subfiles.from: Kazuo Ichihashi for the Japanese Consulate-General, Dublin
subfiles.about: Offers to deliver the official archives and property listed in an earlier inventory and requests travel arrangements for Japanese consular personnel.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum cites repeated and increasingly urgent instructions from the Japanese Foreign Office to complete the surrender. It states that all official property, archives, and keys are ready for delivery at a location designated by the Allies. It also requests facilities and advance notice for the travel of Consul General Setsuya Beppu, Mrs. Beppu, and Consul Kazuo Ichihashi to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Annex I Cross-Reference to the Memorandum of November 12
subfiles.about: Identifies Annex I as a repetition of the Japanese Consulate-General’s November 12 memorandum already transmitted in an earlier despatch.
subfiles.summary: The sheet does not reproduce new substantive text. It explains that Annex I repeats the November 12 memorandum previously forwarded as an enclosure to Despatch No. 2055 of November 14. Its function is to connect the current enclosure set to the earlier record.

subfiles.title: Annex II: Translation of Urgent Instructions from Tokyo
subfiles.from: Japanese Foreign Office, transmitting an Allied Headquarters directive
subfiles.about: Orders the consul general to obey the Allied representative’s directions for immediate surrender and notify the American and British representatives.
subfiles.summary: The translated instruction cites directions issued by Supreme Allied Headquarters in Tokyo on November 26. It orders the consul general to report at once to the American Consulate-General and deliver official archives, property, and keys correctly and without delay. It also requires immediate notification to the American and British representatives that the home-government instruction has been received.

subfiles.title: McEnelly Letter Reporting Beppu’s Unannounced Visit
subfiles.from: Thomas McEnelly, American Consul General, Dublin
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese consul general’s delivery of a memorandum and asks for instructions before taking further action.
subfiles.summary: McEnelly states that Setsuya Beppu appeared without notice and left a communication signed by his subordinate. McEnelly was unable to reach Braddock or Gray immediately but informed Colladay and supplied Braddock with a copy. He notes that Beppu still had not complied with the joint Allied memorandum of November 10 and says he will await Gray’s instructions.

subfiles.title: McEnelly Letter Reporting the Japanese Consul General’s Refusal
subfiles.from: Thomas McEnelly, American Consul General, Dublin
subfiles.about: Describes Beppu’s refusal to accept a renewed American-British order to comply with the November surrender demands.
subfiles.summary: McEnelly summoned Beppu to the consulate, where he appeared with his secretary and refused the communication as exceeding his Tokyo instructions. McEnelly quoted the order requiring compliance with Allied directions, but Beppu demanded to see the American authority and objected to being styled the former Japanese consul general. The letter encloses the rejected instruction.

subfiles.title: Joint American-British Instruction to the Former Japanese Consul General
subfiles.from: Thomas McEnelly and Geoffrey F. Braddock
subfiles.to: Former Japanese Consul General in Dublin
subfiles.about: Directs the former Japanese consul general to comply with the November 10 memorandum and appear with the requested records, articles, and information.
subfiles.summary: The instruction returns the earlier Allied memorandum that the consul general had rejected. It orders him to comply and to appear personally at the American Consulate-General on December 5 at 3:30 p.m. with all specified documents, property, and information. McEnelly signs for the American minister and Braddock for the British representative in Ireland.

subfiles.title: Japanese Memorandum Following the December 4 Conversations
subfiles.about: Restates the consulate’s willingness to surrender property under directions it considers consistent with Tokyo’s wording and asks how repatriation expenses will be paid.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says the consulate will deliver all property and archives when it receives directions conforming to the quoted Tokyo instruction. It insists that actual physical delivery, rather than merely placing the premises under seal, is required. It also asks whether travel expenses for returning personnel will be paid in Dublin, during the journey, or after arrival in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Correction to the Japanese Memorandum of December 5
subfiles.about: Corrects the date of the previous Japanese memorandum cited in the December 5 submission.
subfiles.summary: The slip states that the earlier memorandum referenced on page one should be dated December 3 rather than December 4. It makes no other substantive change. The correction is dated December 6, 1945.

subfiles.title: Departmental Distribution of Despatch No. 2067
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Transmits the Dublin despatch on the Japanese consul general’s refusal to United States intelligence and law-enforcement agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards a copy of confidential Despatch No. 2067 from Dublin. The stated purpose is to provide potentially useful information to military intelligence, naval intelligence, and the FBI. The enclosure concerns the consul general’s refusal to obey surrender orders.

subfiles.title: Copenhagen Airgram on Japanese Archives and Automobiles in Denmark
subfiles.about: Reports that Denmark held no Japanese archives but that two vehicles associated with the Japanese Naval Bureau in Berlin were in British military custody.
subfiles.summary: Checks with Danish and Swedish authorities found no Japanese archives in Copenhagen. Major Floyd Oles reported that a Buick and a Mercedes-Benz, driven into Denmark before Germany’s capitulation to preserve them for the Japanese Naval Bureau, had been seized as war material. The cars were in military use under British control and appeared to be the only Japanese property in Denmark at liberation.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Madrid Concerning Japanese Material in Casablanca
subfiles.about: Authorizes French assumption of custody over Japanese archives and property held by the Spanish consul in Casablanca.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that French custody would accord with paragraph 1(B) of General MacArthur’s directive. It assumes Madrid has not asked the Spanish Foreign Office to make the material available jointly to American, British, and French representatives, as earlier contemplated by Tangier. A copy was sent to Tangier.

subfiles.title: Madrid Airgram Asking Who Should Receive Japanese Material in Casablanca
subfiles.about: Asks whether Japanese archives and property held by the Spanish consul at Casablanca should be requested and transferred to French custody.
subfiles.summary: The airgram invokes paragraph 1(B) of the Department’s October circular telegram. It asks whether the material reported from Casablanca should be requested from the Spanish consul and turned over to the French. A copy was sent to Tangier.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 27,641: Disposition of Japanese Archives and Property in Mexico
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports Four-Power discussions in Mexico and requests clarification of American policy in light of British instructions.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith describes a December 4 meeting with British, Chinese, and Soviet representatives after Sweden exchanged notes with the Mexican Foreign Office. The Soviet representative adopted a difficult position, while the group agreed to seek a detailed accounting from the Swedish minister and meet again after receiving it. Because the British ambassador had instructions favoring shipment of archives to Washington and sale of property, Messersmith asks whether the United States concurs with that policy.

subfiles.title: Geist Memorandum of the Four-Power Meeting in Mexico City
subfiles.about: Records negotiations among American, British, Chinese, and Soviet representatives over obtaining information about Japanese assets held by Sweden.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith explained that Mexico did not object to transfer of the Japanese archives and property to the four powers, distinguishing Japan from Germany because a Japanese government still existed. The British and Chinese representatives supported moving the archives to Washington, while Yakubovski repeatedly demanded direct copies and precise assurances about the proposed correspondence. The meeting eventually agreed that Messersmith would request detailed information on archives, immovable and movable property, funds, accounts, and leases and that Sweden would reply directly to each power.

subfiles.title: British Ambassador’s Letter on Disposal Policy in Mexico
subfiles.from: C. H. Bateman, British Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Provides British proposals for archives, property, funds, and protection work in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Bateman favors moving Japanese archives to Washington with guaranteed British access, ending leases, selling or leasing Japanese-owned buildings, and selling movable official property other than records, stamps, and seals. Proceeds would be administered jointly by the Four Powers, while Sweden could retain necessary funds for protecting Japanese nationals. He notes that unanimity may be required but personally favors majority voting and expects difficulty concerning funds held by the Swedish minister.

subfiles.title: Messersmith’s Request for a Detailed Japanese Asset Statement
subfiles.about: Requests a quadruplicate accounting of all Japanese archives, property, liquid assets, obligations, and leases held by Sweden in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith acknowledges receiving copies of the Swedish and Mexican notes concerning transfer of Japanese interests. Acting for the Four-Power representatives, he asks for descriptions and locations of archives, immovable and movable property, liquid assets, accounts, obligations, and leases. He requests separate copies for the American, British, Soviet, and Chinese diplomatic representatives.

subfiles.title: Swedish Legation Note to the Mexican Foreign Office
subfiles.from: C. H. Petersén, Swedish chargé d’affaires ad interim
subfiles.to: Francisco Castillo Nájera, Mexican secretary of foreign relations
subfiles.about: Notifies Mexico that Sweden has been instructed to transfer Japanese diplomatic and consular property, funds, and archives to Allied representatives while continuing routine protection work.
subfiles.summary: Petersén explains that Japan, through its minister in Stockholm, asked Sweden to comply with Allied requirements by promptly handing over Japanese property, funds, and archives. Sweden would contact representatives of the United States, Great Britain, China, and the Soviet Union and deliver the assets to a jointly selected representative. The Swedish Legation would continue handling routine matters for Japanese nationals pending further instructions.

subfiles.title: Mexican Foreign Office Reply to the Swedish Legation
subfiles.from: Francisco Castillo Nájera, Mexican Foreign Office
subfiles.to: Carl Henrik Gustaf Petersén, Swedish chargé d’affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Sweden’s notice of the proposed transfer of Japanese assets and its continued protection of Japanese nationals in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office recapitulates Sweden’s intention to transfer Japanese diplomatic and consular property, funds, and archives to representatives of the United States, Great Britain, China, and the Soviet Union. It also notes that Sweden will continue routine protection work for Japanese nationals in consultation with those representatives. Castillo Nájera formally acknowledges receipt without raising an objection.
